group.title: Idioms at C1
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A problem or person that is very difficult to deal with or understand.
examples: The final level of the puzzle is {a hard nut to crack}.
wrong: The question was a hard nut to crack, so everyone answered it in seconds.

words.lemma: at the drop of a hat
words.meaning: Immediately and without needing time to think or prepare.
examples: He’d fly to Paris {at the drop of a hat}.
wrong: She agreed at the drop of a hat after thinking about it for months.

words.meaning: To look for a cause or answer in the wrong place, or blame the wrong person.
examples: If you think I took your pen, you’re {barking up the wrong tree}.
wrong: The detective was barking up the wrong tree, so he caught the real thief at once.

words.lemma: get the wrong end of the stick
words.meaning: To misunderstand what someone means or what is happening.
examples: She {got the wrong end of the stick} and thought the party was for her.
wrong: He got the wrong end of the stick, so he understood my point perfectly.
words.ipa: /ɡɛt ðə ˈrɔŋ ˈɛnd əv ðə ˈstɪk/

words.lemma: keep your cards close to your chest
words.meaning: To keep your plans or thoughts secret from other people.
examples: The manager {kept her cards close to her chest} about the new hires.
wrong: He kept his cards close to his chest and told everyone his whole plan.
words.ipa: /ˈkip jɚ ˈkɑrdz ˈkloʊs tə jɚ ˈtʃɛst/

words.lemma: have a chip on your shoulder
words.meaning: To feel angry or bitter because you think you were treated unfairly in the past.
examples: He {has a chip on his shoulder} about not going to college.
wrong: She has a chip on her shoulder, so she feels calm and fairly treated.

words.meaning: To start organizing yourself and behaving in a more sensible, effective way.
examples: You need to {get your act together} before the exams.
wrong: He got his act together and became more disorganized than ever.

words.meaning: To do something too soon, before the right moment.
examples: Let’s not {jump the gun}; the results aren’t final yet.
wrong: He jumped the gun by waiting patiently until everything was ready.

words.meaning: To make someone else deal with a problem you should deal with yourself.
examples: Stop {passing the buck} and fix the mistake yourself.
wrong: She passed the buck and took full responsibility for the error.

words.lemma: the writing is on the wall
words.meaning: There are clear signs that something bad, like failure, will happen soon.
examples: Sales kept falling, and {the writing was on the wall} for the shop.
wrong: The writing was on the wall, so nobody could have guessed the store would close.

words.meaning: Something that has both good and bad results.
examples: Fame can be {a double-edged sword}.
wrong: The plan was a double-edged sword because it had only good effects.

words.meaning: To reach a point where a problem must be dealt with because it is so serious.
examples: The dispute {came to a head} at Monday’s meeting.
wrong: The conflict came to a head and quietly disappeared without anyone noticing.

words.meaning: To avoid becoming close or friendly with someone.
examples: She {keeps her neighbors at arm’s length}.
wrong: He kept her at arm’s length by sharing all his secrets with her.

words.lemma: make a mountain out of a molehill
words.meaning: To treat a small problem as if it were very serious.
examples: It’s only a scratch; don’t {make a mountain out of a molehill}.
wrong: He made a mountain out of a molehill by ignoring a huge disaster.
words.ipa: /ˈmeɪk ə ˈmaʊntən aʊt əv ə ˈmoʊlˌhɪl/

words.meaning: Something that is almost certain to end very badly.
examples: Driving all night with no sleep is {a recipe for disaster}.
wrong: The careful, well-tested plan was a recipe for disaster, so it worked perfectly.

words.lemma: go down like a lead balloon
words.meaning: To be received very badly by other people.
examples: His joke {went down like a lead balloon}.
wrong: The speech went down like a lead balloon, and everyone cheered loudly.

words.meaning: To have a very hard task to do.
examples: With only two days left, we {have our work cut out}.
wrong: We had our work cut out, so the job was very easy.

words.meaning: One small problem that spoils something that is otherwise good.
examples: The hotel was lovely; the only {fly in the ointment} was the noise.
wrong: The fly in the ointment was the best part of the whole trip.

words.meaning: Being planned or prepared and likely to happen soon.
examples: Several new products are {in the pipeline}.
wrong: The project is in the pipeline, so it was finished years ago.

words.meaning: To do many difficult or annoying things to get something.
examples: We had to {jump through hoops} to get the visa.
wrong: Getting the permit was simple; we jumped through hoops in five minutes with no effort.

words.meaning: To finally decide to do something important or risky after thinking about it.
examples: After years of renting, they {took the plunge} and bought a house.
wrong: She took the plunge and decided never to try it.

words.meaning: To try every possible way to find something or solve a problem.
examples: The police {left no stone unturned} in the search.
wrong: They left no stone unturned and stopped looking after one quick try.

words.meaning: Not having the right qualities or skills for a job or activity.
examples: I’m {not cut out for} teaching; I’m too impatient.
wrong: She’s not cut out for nursing, so she is the best nurse in the hospital.

words.meaning: Delayed for now because it is less important than other things.
examples: The new website is {on the back burner} until spring.
wrong: The project is on the back burner, so it’s our top priority today.

words.meaning: Normal and expected, especially when it is not good.
examples: Long delays are {par for the course} at this airport.
wrong: Delays here are par for the course, so they almost never happen.

words.meaning: To go beyond the usual limits and try new things.
examples: The designers love to {push the envelope}.
wrong: The artist pushed the envelope by copying exactly what everyone else did.

words.meaning: To say firmly that something must or must not happen.
examples: When the kids wanted a fourth dessert, I {put my foot down}.
wrong: She put her foot down and let them do whatever they liked.

words.meaning: To cause trouble or upset a calm situation.
examples: He didn’t want to {rock the boat} by complaining.
wrong: She rocked the boat by quietly agreeing with everyone.

words.meaning: Something that takes attention away from the real issue, often on purpose.
examples: The missing key turned out to be {a red herring}.
wrong: The red herring was the most important clue that solved the case.

words.meaning: To choose a less active or less important role.
examples: After retiring, she {took a back seat} in the company.
wrong: He took a back seat and made every decision himself.

words.meaning: People have not yet decided or agreed about something.
examples: {The jury is still out} on whether the new rule works.
wrong: The jury is still out, because everyone already agrees it works.

words.meaning: To stop worrying about risks and do something bold.
examples: We {threw caution to the wind} and booked the trip.
wrong: He threw caution to the wind and checked every risk three times.

words.meaning: To upset someone by getting involved in their area of work.
examples: I don’t want to {tread on anyone’s toes} in the new team.
wrong: She trod on his toes by staying out of his work completely.

words.meaning: Good enough to meet the standard that is needed.
examples: His work isn’t {up to scratch} yet.
wrong: The food was up to scratch, so we sent it back to the kitchen.

words.meaning: Something in the past that no longer matters or causes upset.
examples: We argued years ago, but that’s {water under the bridge} now.
wrong: It’s water under the bridge, so we still argue about it every day.

words.meaning: A painful fact or situation that you have to accept.
examples: Losing the final was {a bitter pill to swallow}.
wrong: Winning the prize was a bitter pill to swallow because it was so pleasant.

words.meaning: To be different from what is normal or natural for you.
examples: Saying nothing {goes against the grain} for her.
wrong: It goes against the grain for him, so he does it happily every day.

words.meaning: To stop doing something that is failing, so you don’t lose even more.
examples: The shop wasn’t working, so we {cut our losses} and closed it.
wrong: He cut his losses by putting even more money into the failing plan.

words.meaning: To just manage to survive, especially with money or work.
examples: With two jobs, they can barely {keep their heads above water}.
wrong: They’re keeping their heads above water, so they are extremely rich.

words.lemma: get off on the wrong foot
words.meaning: To start a relationship or activity badly.
examples: We {got off on the wrong foot}, but now we’re good friends.
wrong: They got off on the wrong foot, so their first meeting was perfect.
